teaches: This opening is one idea wearing a move order: the bishop on the long diagonal, fighting for the central dark squares with pieces instead of pawns — every reply that concedes that diagonal hands the bishop exactly the board it wanted.
explains: The bishop on b2 takes the e5 square in hand down a completely open diagonal. The opponent's modest pawn move promised a central stake it has not yet made — until the pawn arrives on e5, the bishop owns the centre from the wing.

line: b3 d6 Bb2 h5 a3 a5 e3 a4 bxa4
teaches: Flank pawn gestures that are not backed by development are not threats — they are deposits. When the rim pawn offers itself, count what recapturing actually exposes; usually the answer is nothing, and the pawns your opponent marched forward are weaknesses you now own the squares beside.
explains: The pawn on a4 has been taken, and the opponent's opening consists of pawn moves on both rims with no piece developed past the first rank. There is no trick to fear from pieces that have not moved; the material is simply banked and the game continues a pawn up with the better diagonal.
structural: a rim-pawn offer accepted after counting the undeveloped pieces behind it — gestures are not threats
